newsitem.title: UK: Eurotunnel shaky without 50 pct debt cut.
newsitem.headline: Eurotunnel shaky without 50 pct debt cut.

text.p: Channel tunnel operator Eurotunnel SA /Plc's future looks shaky unless it can remove around half of the 9.0 billion pounds ($14.1 billion) wave of debt that has engulfed its operations, analysts said on Tuesday.

The company is still locked in negotiations with its bank creditors, with the spectre of insolvency proceedings in the background, and analysts say half of the debt must disappear for the Anglo-French firm to be a going concern.
"There is one billion pounds of equity, nine billion pounds of debt and 480 million pounds of revenue," said UBS analysts Richard Hannah. "These numbers are just not compatible."

Hannah says that four to five billion pounds of debts must be dealt with in some way for the company to survive and it must also start to resolve the problem of prices on the cross-channel route which have virtually collapsed in the wake of an aggressive price war.
Michael Cohen at Salomon Brothers agreed that around half of the debt must be got rid of in some way.

The problem for the negotiators is that the value of the equity in the company ties their hands when it comes to restructuring its obligations which amount to around nine billion pounds if unpaid interest is added in.
Eurotunnel froze interest payments for 18 months one year ago when the weight of repayments became too much for the company's financial structure to withstand.

The two sides have spent months negotiating and a structure whereby the banks would hold 49 percent of the equity in return for debt has emerged, with other instruments that would cut the cost of servicing the remaining debt also a probability.
The company is said to be insisting that the debt-for-equity swap must be done at a price considerably higher than the current value of the shares, suspended at 113.5p on Monday.
Otherwise the arithmetic just doesn't work.
If, for example, the swap was done at 250p per share, this would only retire just over one billion pounds of the debt.

If another portion was to be swapped for a bond convertible into Eurotunnel shares at a later date, Hannah points out that this would only work if the convertible pays a low interest rate, especially in its early years, and the shares are converted at a relatively low price as an incentive.
A straight debt for bonds swap would only work if this was done at a discount to the value of the debt or at par with a much lower interest rate than Eurotunnel was expected to pay.

The company's outgoing British co-chairman Alister Morton has long argued that it has been paying rates on the debt which are more suited to project finance and now that the business is up and running this fact should be recognised by suitably lower rates since the risk, Morton says, is much reduced.
But the yield on the business has to improve, analysts say.
"The yield is not what was initially expected," Cohen said. "Eurotunnel had to cut prices to get market share. The question is, can they retain customers at higher prices?"
One thing seems clear, and that is that the banks do not want to be saddled with the company's operational headaches by becoming its owners.
This being the case, if a deal is to be done they will take a massive hit on what they are owed, as will the shareholders on the value of their holdings.
But the company will continue to trade with banks receiving some payments and shareholders retaining some value.

"Something has to be better than nothing," as one analyst put it. "If they dress a deal up to make it look as though everyone is sharing the pain to keep the company going and nobody is being wiped out, then it could work." ($1=.6387 Pound)
